# Dockerfile
# Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set environment variables to avoid interactive prompts during package install
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Update package list and install common utilities
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    curl \
    wget \
    git \
    vim \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ONBUILD instructions — triggered automatically when a downstream image
# uses this image as its base (FROM). They do NOT run in this build itself.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Copy the downstream project's source code into /app
ONBUILD COPY . /app

# 2. Ensure any dependencies file is present and install deps if found
#    (generic shell check — override in your downstream image as needed)
ONBUILD RUN if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then \
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3-pip \
                && pip3 install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt \
                && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*; \
            elif [ -f package.json ]; then \
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y nodejs npm \
                && npm install \
                && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*; \
            else \
                echo "No dependency file found — skipping install."; \
            fi

# 3. Set a default environment variable downstream images can override
ONBUILD ENV APP_ENV=production

# 4. Expose a default port (downstream images can override with EXPOSE)
ONBUILD EXPOSE 8080

# Default command
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

content.text:
Updated! Here's what the four `ONBUILD` instructions do — and the key thing to understand is **they fire in the downstream image's build, not this one**:

| # | Instruction | What it does in downstream builds |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ONBUILD COPY . /app` | Copies the downstream project's source into `/app` |
| 2 | `ONBUILD RUN ...` | Auto-detects `requirements.txt` (Python) or `package.json` (Node) and installs deps accordingly |
| 3 | `ONBUILD ENV APP_ENV=production` | Sets a default environment variable; downstream can override it |
| 4 | `ONBUILD EXPOSE 8080` | Declares the default port; downstream can override with their own `EXPOSE` |

**How a downstream image uses this:**
```dockerfile
FROM your-base-image:latest   # ← ONBUILD triggers fire here automatically

# No need to COPY or RUN install — it's already handled!
CMD ["python3", "app.py"]
```

`ONBUILD` is great for base/template images shared across multiple projects — it enforces a consistent structure without requiring each downstream `Dockerfile` to repeat boilerplate. Let me know if you'd like to tune it for a specific stack!

# Dockerfile
# Base image: Ubuntu 22.04 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)
FROM ubuntu:22.04

# Set environment variables to avoid interactive prompts during package install
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Update package list and install common utilities
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
    curl \
    wget \
    git \
    vim \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ONBUILD instructions — triggered automatically when a downstream image
# uses this image as its base (FROM). They do NOT run in this build itself.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Copy the downstream project's source code into /app
ONBUILD COPY . /app

# 2. Ensure any dependencies file is present and install deps if found
#    (generic shell check — override in your downstream image as needed)
ONBUILD RUN if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then \
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y python3-pip \
                && pip3 install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt \
                && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*; \
            elif [ -f package.json ]; then \
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y nodejs npm \
                && npm install \
                && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*; \
            else \
                echo "No dependency file found — skipping install."; \
            fi

# 3. Pull a binary from a remote repository during downstream builds.
#    This script:
#      - Detects the host architecture (amd64 / arm64)
#      - Downloads the matching pre-built binary from GitHub Releases
#      - Verifies the SHA-256 checksum for integrity
#      - Installs it to /usr/local/bin and makes it executable
ONBUILD RUN set -eux; \
    \
    # ── configurable variables ──────────────────────────────────────────── \
    BINARY_NAME="jq"; \
    VERSION="1.7.1"; \
    BASE_URL="https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-${VERSION}"; \
    \
    # ── detect architecture ──────────────────────────────────────────────── \
    ARCH="$(uname -m)"; \
    case "${ARCH}" in \
        x86_64)  ARCH_SUFFIX="amd64" ;; \
        aarch64) ARCH_SUFFIX="arm64" ;; \
        *) echo "Unsupported architecture: ${ARCH}" && exit 1 ;; \
    esac; \
    \
    BINARY_URL="${BASE_URL}/${BINARY_NAME}-linux-${ARCH_SUFFIX}"; \
    CHECKSUM_URL="${BASE_URL}/sha256sum.txt"; \
    \
    echo "==> Downloading ${BINARY_NAME} ${VERSION} for ${ARCH_SUFFIX}..."; \
    curl -fsSL "${BINARY_URL}" -o "/usr/local/bin/${BINARY_NAME}"; \
    \
    # ── verify checksum ──────────────────────────────────────────────────── \
    echo "==> Verifying checksum..."; \
    EXPECTED_CHECKSUM="$(curl -fsSL "${CHECKSUM_URL}" \
        | grep "${BINARY_NAME}-linux-${ARCH_SUFFIX}" \
        | awk '{print $1}')"; \
    ACTUAL_CHECKSUM="$(sha256sum /usr/local/bin/${BINARY_NAME} | awk '{print $1}')"; \
    if [ "${EXPECTED_CHECKSUM}" != "${ACTUAL_CHECKSUM}" ]; then \
        echo "Checksum mismatch! Expected: ${EXPECTED_CHECKSUM}, Got: ${ACTUAL_CHECKSUM}"; \
        rm -f "/usr/local/bin/${BINARY_NAME}"; \
        exit 1; \
    fi; \
    \
    # ── install ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── \
    chmod +x "/usr/local/bin/${BINARY_NAME}"; \
    echo "==> ${BINARY_NAME} ${VERSION} installed successfully."; \
    ${BINARY_NAME} --version

# 4. Set a default environment variable downstream images can override
ONBUILD ENV APP_ENV=production

# 5. Expose a default port (downstream images can override with EXPOSE)
ONBUILD EXPOSE 8080

# Default command
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

content.text:
Done! Here's a breakdown of the new `ONBUILD RUN` shell script (step 3):

### What the script does

```
GitHub Releases (jq v1.7.1)
        │
        ├── 1. Detect CPU arch (x86_64 → amd64, aarch64 → arm64)
        ├── 2. Build the correct download URL for the arch
        ├── 3. curl the binary → /usr/local/bin/jq
        ├── 4. Fetch sha256sum.txt → verify checksum (bail on mismatch 🔒)
        └── 5. chmod +x → confirm with jq --version
```

### Key design decisions

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **`jq`** as the example binary | Real GitHub Release, stable URL pattern, single static binary — easy to swap for any other tool |
| **Arch detection** | Picks `amd64` or `arm64` automatically — works on both x86 servers and Apple Silicon |
| **Checksum verification** | Fetches the official `sha256sum.txt` and compares — catches corrupted or tampered downloads before they land |
| **`set -eux`** | Fails fast on any error (`-e`), prints each command (`-x`), treats unset vars as errors (`-u`) |
| **`curl -fsSL`** | Fails silently on HTTP errors (`-f`), follows redirects (`-L`), suppresses progress noise (`-sS`) |

### Swapping the binary

Just change the top three variables:
```dockerfile
BINARY_NAME="your-tool"
VERSION="x.y.z"
BASE_URL="https://github.com/org/repo/releases/download/v${VERSION}"
```

# 4. Set a default environment variable downstream images can override
ONBUILD ENV APP_ENV=production

# 5. Expose a default port (downstream images can override with EXPOSE)
ONBUILD EXPOSE 8080

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ENTRYPOINT — runs in every child container at startup.
# Uses a wrapper script so we can:
#   - Confirm the execution bit is set on the binary at runtime
#   - Invoke the binary as part of container startup
#   - Then hand off to whatever CMD the child image specifies (exec "$@")
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Write the entrypoint wrapper script into the image
RUN printf '#!/bin/sh\n\
set -e\n\
\n\
BINARY="/usr/local/bin/jq"\n\
\n\
# Ensure the execution bit is set (guard in case layers stripped it)\n\
if [ -f "${BINARY}" ]; then\n\
    chmod +x "${BINARY}"\n\
    echo "[entrypoint] $(${BINARY} --version) is ready."\n\
else\n\
    echo "[entrypoint] WARNING: ${BINARY} not found — skipping."\n\
fi\n\
\n\
# Hand off to the child image CMD (or any docker run arguments)\n\
exec "$@"\n\
' > /usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh \
    && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh

# Register the wrapper as the container entrypoint
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh"]

# Default command passed to the entrypoint (child images can override this)
CMD ["/bin/bash"]

content.text:
Updated. Here's what changed and why each piece matters:

### What was added

**`docker-entrypoint.sh`** — written into the image at build time via `RUN printf ...`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -e

BINARY="/usr/local/bin/jq"

# Re-assert the execution bit at runtime (defensive — some layer
# copy operations or volume mounts can strip permissions)
chmod +x "${BINARY}"
echo "[entrypoint] $(jq --version) is ready."

# Hand off to CMD (or whatever `docker run <image> <cmd>` passes)
exec "$@"
```

**`ENTRYPOINT` + `CMD` split** — this is the idiomatic Docker pattern:

| Instruction | Role |
|---|---|
| `ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh"]` | Always runs first — can't be accidentally overridden by `docker run` args |
| `CMD ["/bin/bash"]` | Default argument passed *into* the entrypoint — child images or `docker run` can replace this freely |

### Why `chmod +x` at runtime too?

The `ONBUILD RUN` already sets the bit during the downstream build, but re-asserting it in the entrypoint is a defensive guard — certain workflows (bind mounts, `COPY --chown`, Windows hosts, or Docker volume overlays) can silently strip executable permissions. The entrypoint catches that before anything tries to run the binary.

### Child container startup flow

```
docker run child-image
      │
      └─► docker-entrypoint.sh runs
              │
              ├── chmod +x /usr/local/bin/jq       ← execution bit guaranteed
              ├── echo "[entrypoint] jq 1.7.1 is ready."
              └── exec /bin/bash  (or child's CMD)  ← hand off
```
